title: Watts and the Man Who Said Hush
description: A playful dog with a surprising talent discovers something strange on a perfectly tidy street.

passages.text: On Maple Close, every house had a pink front door. Every lawn had twelve stripes. Every morning, the neighbors opened their curtains together, waved together, and said, “Lovely day!” Even when it rained. Especially when it rained.

Watts lived at number seven. He was a small golden dog with floppy brown ears and a tail that curled like a question mark. He liked running, sniffing, and discovering things that nobody had meant him to discover.

He discovered a biscuit behind a watering can. He discovered that the cat next door was not a cushion. And he discovered a daisy growing between two perfectly straight paving stones. Watts sniffed it carefully. The daisy was delightfully wonky.

There was something else about Watts. Something you would never guess from watching him scratch his ear. He could turn into a light bulb. Not a dog wearing a lampshade. An actual, floating, shining light bulb.

That afternoon, his friend Nell lost a red boot beneath her porch. “I can see darkness,” she said, peering into the gap. “And possibly a very small dragon.” Watts wagged. He took one breath. Then—plink!—he became a bulb.

Warm light spread beneath the porch. There was the boot, beside a flowerpot. There was a beetle. There was a dusty spoon. There was no dragon, although the beetle looked pleased to have been considered.

Nell reached in and retrieved her boot. “Thank you, Watts.” Plonk! He became a dog again, landed on his paws, and sneezed at the dust. Being a light bulb was useful. Being a dog was better for chasing a ball.

They played until the sky turned peach. Nell threw. Watts fetched. Nell pretended to throw. Watts fetched absolutely nothing, then came back to discuss the matter. Across the street, the lamps began to glow. It was nearly supper time.

Then one streetlamp went out. Then another. A tall man in a plum-colored coat was running along the pavement. He wore a round black hat and carried a sack. He stopped beneath each lamp and whispered, “Hush.”

The golden light curled out of the lamp like a ribbon. Into the sack it went. Watts stopped wagging. That was a bad thing to do. People needed those lights to find their front doors, and beetles had important evening appointments.

The man hurried to a hedge shaped like a bird. He tapped its shadow with one pointed shoe. The shadow fluttered across the pavement, though the hedge did not move at all. It made a quiet, scratchy sound. Shuff. Shuff. Shuff.

Nell took one step closer to her porch. “That isn't how shadows work.” Watts agreed. He barked once. The man turned. Beneath his hat were two sharp eyes and a thin, curling mustache. “No barking,” he said. “Mr Hush requires quiet.”

He whispered at a garden gate. It creaked by itself. He whispered at a doorbell. Instead of ding-dong, it gave a tiny, miserable squeak. Then he scooped the porch light into his sack. The whole street seemed to hold its breath.

Watts's ears drooped. He did not like the shadow's scratching. He did not like the whispering. But he liked Nell, and his neighbors, and this street with its surprising daisy. He could be a little frightened and still do something helpful.

“Stay with your dad,” Watts told Nell in his best, very definite bark. Nell's dad had come to the door. “We'll be right here,” he said. Watts sniffed the pavement. Mr Hush had left a scent like cold dust and old curtains.

Off went Watts, nose down and tail up. Mr Hush slipped through the narrow path between the hedges. Watts followed. Above him, the leaves whispered. Below him, a thin golden thread trailed from a tiny hole in the sack.

The path forked. Cold dust went left. Golden light went left. An extremely interesting sausage smell went right. Watts stopped. He looked right. He looked left. “Later,” he promised the sausage smell, and followed the light.

Something rustled behind him. Watts spun around. A huge shape rose beside the hedge! Two ears! A great round body! It was his own shadow, stretched by the light leaking from the sack. Watts sniffed it. “Oh,” said his little huff.

He kept going. At the end of the path stood the green, with its little clock tower. Every night, its bell told the neighbors it was time to bring their washing in. Mr Hush was hurrying straight toward it.

“One more hush,” the man muttered. “Then every corner dark. Every bell quiet. And I can creep wherever I please.” Watts planted his paws. He could run faster than Mr Hush. But teeth and chasing would not put the lights back.

He needed to shine. Watts remembered Nell's boot. He remembered the beetle and the dusty spoon. Under the porch, his light had shown everything exactly as it was. Perhaps this man liked darkness because he did not want to be seen.

Watts bounded onto the green. Mr Hush reached for the clock tower's little door. “Hush,” he began. Watts took a breath, tucked in his tail, and—PLINK! There, above the grass, floated one very determined light bulb.

Golden light spilled over the green. It lit the daisies. It lit the tower. It lit the pointed shoes, the plum coat, and every curl of that thin mustache. Mr Hush dropped his hand. “Oh,” he said. “That's rather bright.”

Watts shone steadily. He did not need to roar. He did not need to chase. Wherever the warm light touched Mr Hush, a piece of him became see-through. First his shoes. Then his coat. Through his hat, Watts could see a star.

“Hush!” said Mr Hush, but his whisper had become the tiniest puff. His mustache uncurled into a purple ribbon of mist. His hat folded into a speck. Then—fip!—the bad guy disappeared. There was nobody left to say hush.

The sack fell open. Out rushed the stolen light, swirling around Watts like golden streamers. One ribbon flew into a streetlamp. Another slipped under a porch roof. Another hurried down the path, as though it was late for supper.

The strange hedge shadows settled where they belonged. The garden gate stopped creaking. A doorbell tried its voice. “Ding,” it said. Then, much more confidently, “DONG!” Above the green, the clock bell rang a bright, ordinary, beautiful BONG.

Plonk! Watts was a dog again. Four paws. Two floppy ears. One excellent nose. Nell came down the path with her dad. “There you are!” she called. Watts ran to meet her so fast that his ears streamed behind him.

All along Maple Close, doors opened. Neighbors stepped outside at different times. One laughed. One asked what had happened. Someone brought biscuits. The lady at number four sat on her garden chair, which was just a little crooked, and did not straighten it.

“He brought the lights back,” Nell said, hugging Watts. Watts accepted a biscuit. Then he remembered the sausage smell. He led them along the path to a neighbor bringing a plate indoors. A little plain piece was saved especially for him.

They walked home beneath the glowing lamps. Nell skipped. Her dad whistled. Watts visited the wonky daisy between the paving stones. It was still there, leaning whichever way it liked. He touched it gently with his nose and wagged his curly tail.

At number seven, Nell put both red boots by the door. Watts circled his bed once, twice, and settled with a sigh. The street was bright again. His people were close. He did not have to shine every minute. Sometimes, a dog could simply sleep.

scenes.alt: Watts the golden dog explores a perfectly tidy suburban street.
Watts becomes a glowing light bulb to help a child find a red boot under a porch.
Watts watches a mysterious man steal warm light from the tidy street.
Watts follows the mysterious man through a narrow hedge path toward the village green.
Watts shines as a light bulb, making the spooky man disappear on the green.
Watts runs home through a warmly lit neighborhood as neighbors enjoy the evening.
